title: Everything connected (Laudato Si')
hookLine: read a section on the connection of all creatures
tomorrow: how is a trip to the market a step toward holiness?

lines: A LONG CHAIN IN YOUR HAND.
cards: The phone in your hand holds metal dug out of the ground somewhere far away, assembled by hands you'll never meet, charged by power from a plant you've never seen.
Every ordinary object is a long chain of places and people. So here's the question: can you love the planet and ignore the person next to you?
Pope Francis answers it in Laudato Si', his letter on care for our common home, in a short section called a universal communion.

teach.b: His answer: no. Everything is connected. The letter's name comes from the song of Francis of Assisi, his canticle, which praises God through brother sun, sister moon and our sister, mother earth.
Pope Francis says he's writing to every person living on this planet, not only Catholics. Then he ties three knots.
Every creature is bound to God; he borrows a line from the book of Wisdom calling the Lord a lover of the living.

teach.h: BOUND TO GOD, BOUND TO EACH OTHER.
teach.b: Creatures are bound to each other, like brothers and sisters on one pilgrimage.

teach.h: THE EARTH'S CRY, THE POOR'S CRY.
teach.b: And care for the earth is bound to care for people. A feeling of communion with nature, he says, can't be real if the heart has no tenderness for other human beings.

He finds it strange to fight the trafficking of endangered animals and stay indifferent to the trafficking of people. Elsewhere he hears two cries as one: the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor.
A neighbor tradition says something close.
In the Qur'an, in Pickthall's English: "The seven heavens and the earth and all that is therein praise Him, and there is not a thing but hymneth His praise; but ye understand not their praise."
Muslims and Catholics both hear creation as a choir turned toward God. The difference is honest.
Francis's letter reads creation through Christ, whom Catholics believe is God made flesh; Muslims honor Jesus as a prophet, not as God.

how: Readers of Laudato Si' take it as a call to care for creation and for the poor together, in prayer and in practical work.

o: a belief that all living things share a single soul
creatures bound to God, to each other, and to people
a teaching that nature matters more than people do

p: names from Francis of Assisi's canticle
heard alongside the cry of the poor

s: Laudato Si' is a letter about nature, not about people
Francis says communion with nature isn't real without tenderness for other human beings.
Pope Francis addressed Laudato Si' to every person living on the planet
not only Catholics: he says so near the start.
the Qur'an and Francis's canticle both picture creation praising God
not a thing but hymneth His praise, says the Qur'an; the canticle praises God through brother sun.

games.q: your class is planning an earth day cleanup, and someone suggests skipping the block with the homeless camp because it's 'not environmental.' what would Laudato Si' say?
o: skip it; the letter is about animals and plants.
include it, with care for the people there: earth and poor are one cry.
only clean there if the people living there leave first.
games.why: Francis hears the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor together. care for creation that ignores people isn't the communion he describes.

practice: Rest your eyes on one ordinary thing near you, a glass of water, a piece of bread, the chair under you, and trace it back a few steps: the hands, the soil, the rain behind it. Stay in that web without judging it.
If you pray, give thanks for one link in the chain.

wordCard.voice: Everything connected. The thread of Laudato Si': creatures bound to God and to each other, and care for the earth bound to care for people.

orig.note: Old Umbrian Italian, not Latin: praise be to you, the first words of Francis of Assisi's canticle.

carryVoice: Your line: connected. The cry of the earth and the cry of the poor come as a pair. Till tomorrow, then.

sources.work: Francis of Assisi, Canticle of the Creatures
